questions.q: What commonly breaks when a model is served by simply loading it at import time and calling model.predict() inside a single Flask route?
options: Concurrent requests hit one process serially, there's no clean way to roll out a new model version without dropping requests, and every model needs its own hand-rolled plumbing
Flask cannot run on Linux containers
Python cannot import machine learning libraries at all
GPUs are physically incompatible with web frameworks
questions.explain: A hand-rolled Flask wrapper has no request batching, no clean versioning/rollout story, and no shared plumbing across models — exactly what real serving frameworks solve generically.

questions.q: What is NVIDIA Triton Inference Server?
options: A Kubernetes CRD that only KServe can create
A multi-framework serving runtime (TensorRT, PyTorch, ONNX, Python backends) with dynamic batching and multi-model hosting built in
A tool exclusively for training models, not serving them
A managed database for storing model weights
questions.explain: Triton is a serving runtime that supports multiple frameworks and backends, with dynamic batching and multi-model/multi-version hosting as built-in features.

questions.q: How does KServe relate to a predictor like Triton or TorchServe?
options: KServe is a lower-level replacement for the GPU driver stack
KServe runs only on bare-metal servers and cannot use Kubernetes

KServe sits above the predictor on Kubernetes, generating the Deployment, Service, Ingress, and autoscaling around it and standardizing the request protocol, while Triton or TorchServe can run underneath as the actual model server
KServe and Triton are mutually exclusive; a cluster can only use one or the other across its entire fleet
questions.explain: KServe is a Kubernetes-native layer (via the InferenceService CRD) that provisions and standardizes the surrounding infrastructure, while a predictor like Triton or TorchServe can run underneath it as the engine actually executing the model.

questions.q: What is vLLM specifically built for?
options: General-purpose CPU-only batch scoring
Replacing Kubernetes Ingress controllers
Storing experiment-tracking metadata
High-throughput large language model serving, using techniques like PagedAttention and continuous batching
questions.explain: vLLM targets LLM-specific serving throughput, using PagedAttention and continuous batching to outperform generic serving frameworks on that particular workload.

questions.q: In the lesson's minimal InferenceService YAML example, what infrastructure does KServe generate automatically that is notably absent from the spec itself?
options: The model's training data
The Deployment, Service, Ingress, and autoscaling resources needed to actually run and expose the predictor
The GPU driver installed on the node
The cloud provider's billing account
questions.explain: The InferenceService spec only declares the predictor and its storage location; KServe generates the underlying Deployment, Service, Ingress, and autoscaling configuration itself.
